en: The Sage, whose eyes are like blossoming lotuses, whose face is like the moon, and whose hair is like black bees; who resembles perfectly purified and melted gold; who possesses a halo of light like the sky;
and whose lotus-feet are touched by the crowns of Śakra, Brahmā, Kubera, and Māra.
I pay homage to the Buddha, the sun, pure and stainless, the source of the rays of the true Dharma.
From that great sun of a Buddha, whose radiance is spread by knowledge, those rays of the true Dharma have issued forth and shine through all directions.
Homage to that Dharma, by which this world, though perpetually asleep, is awakened to reality; and having realized it, the sages attain tranquility.
That which is heard to have been thus awakened by those very ones, emitted like the sun by the Tathāgatas—[to that Dharma, homage].

With devotion, I worship the vast grove of lotuses that is the Saṅgha upon this earth: fragrant with the scent of morality, possessing pure petals, with the factors of enlightenment as its beautiful stalks, containing the cool water of the purity of the dhyānas and formless attainments, and having Nirvāṇa as its excellent pericarp. 5.1.3
For from the four elements, like snakes gathered in a single vessel,
whichever one becomes enraged, that very one brings about harm.
[It is] unstable, unhappy, without self, impure, essence-less, ungrateful, and uncontrollable.
He who perceives the body as "I" and "mine" is deceived and wanders in delusion.
(5.1.5) [It is] a machine of suffering with hundreds of nests for swarms of worms, ungrateful,
and a constant target for hundreds of arrows of calamity.
Who that is wise and possessed of revulsion would take delight here in this body, which constantly flows with nine impure channels, being transformed and unclean like the froth upon water? 5.1.6
In this body, which is subject to death and the locus of disease and old age, and which destroys all that has been done when it perishes— how can you allow your mind to become attached to it? (5.1.7)
When, having cast off the body, one goes helplessly along a well-tended path that is nonetheless leaderless and terrifying, accompanied only by one's own past conduct—
then for the sake of what do you not practice self-restraint, intent as you are on the adornment of the body?
Like one condemned to death at the moment of his execution, he was seized by supreme fear,
for he was constantly surrounded by four beings who were not provoked by enmity yet remained hostile, like four venomous serpents.
Therefore, this body has been described by the Sugata as an anthill, full of many fears and great terrors,
because it is riddled with many cavities and grows gradually. 5.1.9
Filled with many various swarms of worms,
easily struck down by manifold blows, and devoid of self,
this body is therefore called an anthill.
Just as on earth a mound of clay is called an anthill because it has been brought forth from the body of a worm,
so too is this [body] a drop of impurity produced by a father and mother.

One who has awakened in this world [should realize] that it is merely a body. (5.1.11) Indeed, a wise person should not harbor pride on account of physical form, power and wealth, or even intellectual acumen.
For he sleeps at the proper time upon the ground,
crushed like an anthill by an elephant in a fit of rut. [He knows] the exhalation, the inhalation, the opening of the eyes, and the closing of the eyes.
Having observed that suffering born of standing, walking, lying down, and sitting is ever forcibly present within material bodies, who would resort to this misfortune called "body"? (5.1.13)
The four elements— earth, water, fire, and air— which reside within the body,
have been cherished with various comforts such as bathing, anointing, and food; yet,
when even slightly slighted, they become merciless and abandon everything that has been done for them.
When enraged, they strike down like most venomous snakes when touched;
yet ascetics who wander with discernment are not bitten by them. For even if someone were bitten by a poisonous snake, death would not occur if there are mantras and medicines.
But when bitten everywhere by these four uneven spirits, which are unrestrained and consist of mutual delusion, the world becomes bewildered and does not attain peace.
Just as in a great target, [arrows] are released even without effort, so it is here.
Spears, rocks, and arrows become unfailing; likewise, various misfortunes—cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, clods of earth, and sticks—fall upon the body. (5.1.16)
When this body is produced from the impure semen of the father and the blood of the mother, arising here gradually like a fruit from a seed,
it is merely covered by a thin skin, having disregarded its own innate nature.
How does passion for the body arise in you? It does not arise through right understanding.
One should not eat for the sake of pride, nor for [the sake of] vanity; one should consume food, whether it possesses qualities or lacks them, solely for the purpose of maintaining the body.
For food certainly sustains the body here in this world by virtue of its inherent nature,
just as support is given to a house whose foundations have become unstable and weak.
This body is thus incessantly oppressed and lacks autonomy.
Like a weak cart shattered by enemies such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst, old age, and the like, it is maintained and driven by various kinds of specialized equipment. (5.1.19)
Why do you indulge in this vulgar pride of youth while standing at the very mouth of old age?
Why do you take pride in health when the bodily constituents are the very seat of disease?
Why, out of delusion, do you take pride in life when you stand upon the tip of Death’s hand?
Why do you have these three intoxications when there are three terrifying calamities for one who is great?

He who, with a joyful heart, having cut the skin from his own body, quickly made it into birch-bark, and from his own body likewise made his hand into a brush and the blood, shining like the bandhujīva flower, into ink; || 5.1.20 ||
"He who, for the sake of eloquent speech before his awakening, split open his own body with a bone and fashioned a pen resembling white silver—he, indeed, that best of sages, spoke this Sūtra.
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:"

§2 It is just as, monks, with a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of atimuktaka flowers, or a garland of vārṣika jasmine—whether worn on the body, on clothing, or placed in a vessel—which, as those various nights and days pass by, and as those various moments, instants, and hours elapse, surely decays, surely withers, and surely dries up.

Monks, there comes a time when that garland of blue lotuses, or garland of campaka flowers, or garland of atimuktaka flowers, or garland of vārṣika jasmine—whether it has come from Aṅga, or is made of cloth, or is placed upon a vessel—after the passing of various nights and days, and after the passing of various moments, instants, and hours, becomes withered, faded, and dried up, until it is entirely reduced to a heap of refuse.

"In the same way, monks, this body too is material, gross, composed of the four great elements, born from the impurity of the mother and father's *kalala*, nourished by rice and gruel, and subject to constant rubbing, bathing, massaging, breaking, scattering, and destruction. With the passing of various nights and days, and with the passing of various moments, instants, and hours, it simply decays, withers, dries up, and dies."

Monks, there comes a time when this body—material, gross, composed of the four great elements, born from the impurity of the mother and father's kalala, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to constant rubbing, bathing, and massaging, yet liable to breaking, scattering, and destruction—after the passing of various nights and days, and after the passing of various moments, instants, and hours, becomes worn out, withered, dried up, and dead, ending entirely in the cemetery.

§4. Monks, when one has died and passed away, his kinsmen either burn the body with fire, or cast it into water, or bury it in the earth, or various creatures belonging to the animal realm devour it; or else it undergoes complete drying up, destruction, and exhaustion by wind and sun. Yet as for that which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness"— [The remainder of the paragraph follows: ...that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here after death, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a great tree that has been cut down at its root: although the branches and twigs may still be there, they wither and dry up. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a river flowing toward the ocean: once it has reached the ocean, it cannot be pointed out as being "here" or "there. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a seed sown in a field: depending on the soil and the rain, it grows, flourishes, and comes to fruition. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a flame blown by the wind: it goes out and cannot be pointed out as being "here" or "there. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a person who, having borrowed goods from another, returns them when asked. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a person who, having committed an offense against the king, flees to a border region and lives there. In the same way, monks, when one has died and passed away, that mind, intellect, or consciousness does not remain here, nor does it go elsewhere. It is just like a person who, having committed an offense against the king, is bound with ropes and taken away. It is just like a person who, having committed an offense against the king, is struck by a spark of fire. In the same way

That [mind], having been cultivated for a long time through faith, and cultivated through ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom, becomes upward-tending, distinguished, and leads to heaven in the future. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Why are you so intent on the act of adorning the body?
Do not, out of delusion, fail to strive in wholesome deeds;
for when impermanence seizes it away, it will take this [body] from you.
Like a nurse embracing a young prince with her arms and lap—
though provided with clothing, food, drink, beds, and seats, and though cherished with baths, ointments, and ornaments.

For this body, out of ingratitude, does not follow anyone for even a moment as they depart for the next world— [that person] who, having obtained this rare convergence of favorable conditions, [neglects it].
Regarding the body, he does not think of his own welfare;
like a prince renouncing a royal consecration, he abandons that very body and departs for his true purpose. (5.3.3)
Though served like a teacher, though nourished like a son, though looked upon like a kinsman, and though honored like a master,
the fickle body departs after striking out, like a monkey.
Having abandoned it, he could not endure even a single committed transgression.
[This applies] to those of haughty nature and great lineage who are proud of their ancestry,
as well as to those of tranquil soul whose fortune has been eclipsed.

When life has ceased, these bodies— cast aside with their arms, feet, and necks— attain a state of equality; for even a brahmin, though proud of his lineage, learning, and beauty, becomes like one filled with revulsion.
And a caṇḍāla is indeed to be shunned by the world;
yet in such a world, where both lie together upon the funeral pyre in the course of time, who indeed could feel pride? (5.3.6)
Having obtained this body through tenfold virtuous action, why, being addicted to pleasure— namely, the pleasure of sensual desire— do you not perform meritorious deeds?
Seek the fruit from this body, which is unstable and essence-less, just as one seeks wealth from a hired laborer who receives a vast wage;
for this body is like a city of filth.
Nourished in the womb by impure food-essence within impurity, therefore, even though it is endowed with a body, it must be abandoned by the wise, like a lotus born from foul water. 5.3.8
Though guarded like a son, though nurtured, and though cherished with baths, garments, and ornaments,
the body nonetheless abandons, destroys, and strikes down [its master].
Having abandoned it after it has been well-maintained, one is like an ungrateful thief;
for this body, though protected for a very long time from water, fire, wind, disease, enemies, and wild beasts, ends in dissolution.

At the time of death, it brings torment like a borrowed garment made of worthless material being torn away from one who has not acquired its substance. Having destroyed prosperity, though it was easily obtained through wholesome qualities—
Driven by that body toward the cause of sensual pleasure,
he— having burned the finest aloe-wood for the sake of a single measure of rice— is tormented like an ignorant Śabara who has failed in his purpose. 5.3.11
He who abandons the supreme bliss, the unassailable, and the peaceful path, and instead seeks the ignoble pleasure of the senses through toil,
becomes one who has fallen away and is an object of derision in the world.
Like one who,

fearing the disfigurement of the body, does not observe the rules of discipline even while looking upon death as if it were a blazing forest fire, he merely colors his soiled, ragged garment with saffron.
That fool sleeps here, consumed by grief for not having attained his own goal,
like a yak whose tail-tip has caught fire in a forest conflagration.
(5.3.13) As long as the lunar chariot is beautiful with swans, lotus fibers, jasmine, and crystal slabs...

As long as the solar chariot, with its blazing mass of rays and spreading beams, continues to shine, may the righteous Wheel of Dharma born from the mouth of the One Possessing Ten Powers— whose sharp edge is wisdom—
cut through the suffering of the world arising from the creeper of craving and causing manifold fears. 5.3.14
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether dwelling upon the earth or in the atmosphere,
may they always maintain loving-kindness toward all creatures.
And let them practice the Dharma by day and by night. || 5.3.15
